20 SIGNATURES. ONE PROOF.
Daisugi v0.3 aggregates 20 transaction signatures using LeanSPHINCS and LeanVM.
20 SPHINCS signatures are verified through a single aggregate proof.
For EL clients, verification requires the LeanVM verifier plus the LeanSPHINCS guest program.
Post quantum signature aggregation is live on Daisugi. Kudos to @Nethermind @Gianluca_Felli

Daisugi v0.2 now supports Frame Transactions.
SPHINCS signed transactions can run as native frames, with per frame execution and verification, alongside the existing ERC 4337 flow.
Same post quantum signatures. New transaction model.
Next: signature aggregation via LeanSPHINCS.

text:
The sudden collapse of the value of CoT (even summarized CoT) in the agentic era changes working with AI.

Effectively steering AIs and getting any sort of observability now requires you to ask for interim outputs & tests, and to use AI help to troubleshoot problems you find.

It used to be that you could look at the CoT from a request and get a sense of where the model was going, but with tons of agents calling other agents, and CoTs that run to thousands of pages for even simple agentic tasks, that is no longer possible.

It also requires you to trust the orchestrator model more than ever, since it is the only thing that can track all of the tasks. Which means you need to use AI to both find problems with AI and to troubleshoot problems you find.

United Airlines says that last month, more than 5.4 million people - about a third of United's customers - had @Starlink on their flight and that satisfaction scores are more than 40 points higher on Starlink-equipped planes than those with other Wi-Fi service.

New opinion article about @Starlink from a 7-year Delta Airlines Diamond Medallion status member (their highest loyalty tier):

"After flying a United flight in July that included Starlink, it was enough reason for me to switch. It was amazing, like being on the internet at my house, that's how fast it is. For the two-hour flight, I was just doing work. As a founder, I don't get the luxury of being able to log off for a few hours in the middle of the day. When Slack and email are going, or I'm collaborating and working with teammates, or I'm building an app, I want to have fast internet.

On most Delta flights that I'm on, there's at least some segment of the flight during which the internet goes out for a period of time, whether for a few minutes or 20 minutes. The reliability of the uptime leaves a bit to be desired. Nearly all of Delta's peers went with Starlink, while Delta went with Amazon's Leo, which won't be out until 2028.

I hope Delta takes stock of all the online chatter and listens to its customers. It has done a great job in the past of continually improving its product and listening to its customers. For the most profitable and what I feel is the most premium airline in America, it seems odd for Delta not to outfit its planes with the best in-flight internet."

I think we'll see more and more stories like this. As people get a taste of Starlink wi-fi on planes, they won't want to go back, and will demand better internet from airlines that don't have it, and in some cases, just switch to flying other airlines that do have it.

text:
My biggest obsession right now is doing work with my AirPods in: walking and talking to a "coordinator" agent who can do tasks in parallel.

When I'm sitting at a desk, my left brain is activated.
I'm in logic and facts and procedure mode.
When I'm walking, I activate more of the right brain. Something about moving the body lifts my spirit. I'm not only more creative... I also have more energy. My mood is lifted, and I can think more clearly. I even write better while walking.

This has been a habit of mine for 2 years now. I would take voice memos while on walks, and then, when I returned to my desk, I would have a "plan." Well, now I can literally do things while walking. My agent (Dot, currently the best real-time voice agent) can spin up local Codex sessions on my computer, is connected to all my tools, and can communicate with anyone on my team. All by simply talking.

(sent via Riley's Dot using the x-api skill)

This is obviously the future of video games. 

Streamers and their community building the game together, then playing it. 

When Astra came out I streamed a call of duty clone, with 10 loadouts, vehicles, kill streaks etc, and in between matches people we're shouting in the voice chat (that we vibe coded into the game), what changes they wanted. 

But i see a world where they can send in their prompts and the team of the streamer can moderate those prompts and send them through, and the agents will make 20 changes at once, and then 30 min later everyone could be playing the next version of the game. 

And every month that goes by, as models improve, these games will look more and more professional. Some company will figure out how to make these games easily forkable, hostable, monetizable, social, fast, and fun.
